en: During Amihan, cool and dry northeast winds from Siberia bring clear skies and lower temperatures to the Philippines between November and February.
The reddish-brown laterite soil found in many Philippine provinces gets its distinct color from high concentrations of oxidized iron minerals.
The towering cliffs of El Nido, Palawan, are made of coral limestone, a sedimentary rock formed from ancient marine organism remains.
In coastal Philippine towns, a sea breeze forms in the afternoon when land heats faster than the ocean, causing air to rise.
Venus appears as the brightest object in the evening sky, often called the Evening Star, because its thick clouds highly reflect sunlight.
Observers in the Philippines cannot see Polaris, the North Star, because it sits directly above Earth's northern pole, below their horizon.
Because the Moon orbits Earth, it rises approximately fifty minutes later each successive night, shifting its visible position in the sky.
Satellite images show that typhoons in the Philippines always rotate counterclockwise due to the Coriolis effect caused by Earth's rotation.
Pumice from Philippine volcanoes like Taal is a lightweight rock full of gas bubbles that can float on water.
Tall, anvil-shaped cumulonimbus clouds frequently build up over Philippine mountains in the late afternoon, triggering heavy rain and lightning storms.
Banana plants in Philippine backyards release significant amounts of water vapor into the air through transpiration from their large leaves.
The Sierra Madre mountain range blocks moisture-laden winds, creating a rain shadow effect that keeps central Luzon relatively dry.
